verdicts.summary: Lean has an equivalent formula. The Lean never writes a limsup: `limsup` and `limSup` occur nowhere in NavierStokes/ (only in Euler/, which is out of scope). The clause is encoded as the quantifier unfolding `SpeedUnboundedAtOne u` = ∀ M > 0, ∀ δ > 0, ∃ t ∈ (0,1) with 1-δ < t and ∃ x with M < ‖u(t,x)‖. Recovery, both directions: for g(t) := ‖U(t)‖_{L^∞} with values in [0,∞], limsup_{t↑1} g(t) = ∞ holds iff for every M and every δ there is t ∈ (1-δ,1) with g(t) > M, which is the Lean statement once `∃ x, M < ‖u(t,x)‖` is identified with `sup_x ‖u(t,x)‖ > M`. That identification is the one encoding choice: the paper's L∞(T³) norm is an essential supremum over the torus, the Lean takes the pointwise Euclidean norm of the value at a single lifted point x ∈ ℝ³. They agree because U(t,·) is continuous (ContDiffOn on preSingularDomain) and 1-periodic in each coordinate (UnitSpatialPeriodsOn (Ico 0 1) u), so the lift's pointwise supremum equals the torus essential supremum; a point of the open set where the norm exceeds M has positive measure. The Lean also pins t to the open interval (0,1), matching `t ↑ 1` from below, and quantifies δ so the witnesses accumulate at 1 — the same content. `unbounded_speed_excludes_uniform_bound` (ProblemStatement.lean:159) confirms the intended reading: the condition contradicts any uniform bound ‖u(t,x)‖ ≤ C on [0,1) × ℝ³.
